terms.short: Steamed dumplings filled with spiced minced beef, topped with garlic yogurt and a carrot-pea qorma.
terms.long: Wheat dumplings steamed and stuffed with spiced minced beef and onion, served topped with a garlic-yogurt sauce, a tomato-based carrot-and-pea qorma, and a dusting of dried mint and cayenne. Both dairy and meat toppings are always present, not optional. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia).

spicy.note: A dusting of cayenne on top; usually mild unless requested hotter.

terms.short: Steamed dumplings filled with leek and scallion, topped with garlic yogurt and a minced-beef-lentil qorma.
terms.long: The vegetarian-filled cousin of mantu: wheat dumplings stuffed with leek and scallion rather than meat, but still topped with garlic yogurt and — in the traditional presentation — a minced beef and lentil qorma sauce, so the dish as typically served is not vegetarian overall despite the filling being vegetable. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia).

contains.specific: leek, scallion filling; garlic in the yogurt
minced beef in the qorma topping
contains.note: A vegetarian version without the meat topping may be available on request — worth asking.

terms.ask: Can the aushak come without the meat qorma topping, if I want it vegetarian?

terms.short: The general Afghan word for a braised stew — herb-and-yogurt or tomato-based, distinct from Indian korma's nut-cream base.
terms.long: A broad category of slow-braised stews in Afghan cooking, built variously on fresh herbs (sabzi), split peas (nakhoud), or tomato, usually finished with a little yogurt. Despite the name overlap, Afghan qorma is not the same dish as Indian korma — it is not typically thickened with nut paste, and the flavor profile is herbier and less sweet. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia, offering many qorma varieties by protein and style).

terms.short: Afghanistan's national dish — basmati rice baked with lamb, topped with caramelized carrot and raisin, sometimes almond.
terms.long: Basmati rice cooked in lamb broth and baked, topped with a sweet-savory garnish of julienned carrot slow-cooked with sugar until caramelized, and raisins, occasionally with slivered almond scattered on top as well. The carrot-raisin topping is standard; almonds are a common but not universal addition. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia).

contains.specific: lamb, cooked into the rice and broth

contains.note: A common but not universal topping — visible and removable when present.

terms.ask: Does this qabuli have almonds on top?

terms.short: Skewered, char-grilled meat — lamb, beef, or chicken, marinated simply and grilled plain, not sauced.
terms.long: Cubed or ground meat threaded on skewers and grilled over charcoal, seasoned simply with salt, pepper, and sometimes yogurt or ground coriander in the marinade — much less spiced than Indian or Levantine kebabs. Usually served over rice or bread with grilled tomato. Nut-free and mild. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia, offering lamb tenderloin, chops, beef tenderloin, and ground beef/chicken kabobs).

contains.note: Beef and chicken are equally standard skewer choices.

terms.short: Fried eggplant slices in tomato sauce, topped with garlic yogurt and dried mint.
terms.long: Eggplant sliced and fried until soft, layered with a tomato-garlic sauce, and finished with a cool garlic yogurt drizzle and dried mint. A standard vegetarian side or appetizer. Dairy is a defining topping, not optional.

terms.short: Sweet-savory braised pumpkin, finished with garlic yogurt and a meat or split-pea sauce.
terms.long: Pumpkin or butternut squash braised until soft with a little sugar, giving a sweet-savory profile, topped with garlic yogurt and often a meat sauce (qorma) similar to how mantu and aushak are finished. Vegetarian versions swap in split peas for the meat topping.

contains.specific: meat qorma topping, in the non-vegetarian version
contains.note: A split-pea (nakhoud) vegetarian version is standard.

terms.short: Unleavened flatbread stuffed with mashed potato, leek, or pumpkin, pan-fried until crisp.
terms.long: A thin wheat dough folded flat around a filling — potato and scallion, leek, or pumpkin are the standard choices — and pan-fried or griddled until the outside crisps, served with yogurt and sometimes a cilantro-chili sauce. Vegan by default (no meat, no dairy in the bread or filling), though the yogurt dip served alongside adds dairy.

contains.note: The bread itself is dairy-free; the standard accompaniment is not.

terms.short: Split lentils or peas simmered simply with turmeric and cumin — a plain, mild side.
terms.long: Yellow split peas or lentils simmered until soft with turmeric, cumin, and a little tomato, milder and less spiced than most Indian dal preparations. Vegan and nut-free as a rule.

terms.short: Rice cooked in a milk-based broth, giving a pale, creamy-tasting pilaf despite containing no cream.
terms.long: A specialty rice preparation cooked in milk rather than water or stock, giving the grains a pale color and a subtly creamy flavor without added cream or butter beyond the milk itself. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia, listed among the chef's specials).

contains.note: Not obvious from the name — the rice itself is cooked in milk.

terms.short: Clear, simple meat and vegetable broth soup — chicken, veal, or lamb shank.
terms.long: A plain, home-style clear broth soup with chunks of meat (chicken, veal, or lamb shank) and root vegetables, lightly seasoned. One of the mildest, simplest items on an Afghan menu, and a vegetarian version is standard too. From real DC-area menus (Bistro Aracosia).

contains.note: Veal, lamb shank, and vegetarian versions are equally standard.
